name: Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex)
summary: One or two short gyri running transversely across the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus, hidden inside the Sylvian fissure. They receive the acoustic radiation from the medial geniculate body and hold a tonotopic map (low frequencies anterolaterally, high frequencies posteromedially). Because the auditory pathway is bilateral from the brainstem up, a unilateral lesion never causes deafness, only subtle deficits in localization and in perceiving speech in noise; bilateral lesions produce cortical deafness or pure word deafness. The planum temporale behind Heschl's gyrus is larger on the left in most people and merges into Wernicke's area.

anatomy.location: On the superior (opercular) surface of the superior temporal gyrus within the depths of the lateral sulcus, running obliquely backward and medially from the lateral surface toward the insula; the planum temporale lies posterior to it.

function: Conscious perception of sound, frequency and intensity analysis, sound localization and the first cortical stage of speech and music perception.

bestView.label: Heschl's gyrus on the upper surface of the temporal lobe inside the Sylvian fissure
transverse gyrus running toward the insula

imaging.normalAppearance: Seen on coronal T1 as the transverse gyrus on the roof of the temporal lobe, medial to the Sylvian fissure and lateral to the insula; on axial images it runs obliquely toward the posterior insula. Bilateral infarcts here are the classic cause of cortical deafness.

pathology.pathology: Bilateral temporal infarcts with cortical deafness
pathology.finding: Bilateral superior temporal restriction, typically from sequential MCA strokes.
Focal lesion of the superior temporal gyrus with ictal buzzing or ringing.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; FLAIR; audiometry and brainstem auditory evoked responses (preserved in cortical deafness)

lesionEffects.deficit: Mild contralateral hearing loss and impaired localization
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the predominantly crossed cortical input

lesionEffects.deficit: Cortical deafness or pure word deafness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral Heschl's gyri or their radiations with preserved brainstem responses

examination: Whisper test and localization of sounds
Ask about hearing in noisy rooms
Repetition of spoken words versus reading (pure word deafness spares reading)
pearls: A deaf ear is never a cortical sign
Pure word deafness: the patient hears but cannot understand speech, yet reads and writes normally
